faqs.q: Groundhogs are damaging my Smithsburg orchard ground — what is the approach?
faqs.a: Orchard groundhogs are trapped as a system, not as individuals. Burrows under the packing sheds and along the orchard's edge rows connect, and a mature system can run across several properties' fence lines. We map the entrances, trap the active system through the season — early work, before the year's young disperse, gives the longest relief — and backfill and screen the buildings once the system is empty. Burrow entrances in the rows themselves get collapsed and marked for the mowing crews. On producing ground the goal is a managed perimeter: the mountain woods will always hold groundhogs, and the orchard's buildings and rows are what we defend.

Mountain-side properties add access time on steep, wooded lots. Smithsburg.wildlife_intro:
Smithsburg is a small town in the orchard country of northeastern Washington County, tucked against South Mountain where the fruit farms climb the slopes and the Appalachian Trail runs along the ridge above town. The elevation and the orchards shape its wildlife: this is bat, raccoon, and groundhog country with a mountain edge.

Groundhogs burrow the orchard rows and field edges and under the barns and sheds of the fruit farms, and the deer that browse the orchards are the town's famous background animal. Raccoons den in the chimneys of the older in-town homes and in the hollow trees of the mountain woods interchangeably. Bats summer in the farmhouse attics and the older rooflines in town, feeding over the orchards at dusk. The rocky mountain ground holds copperheads, and timber rattlesnakes live along the South Mountain ridge — protected animals, safety and referral only. Smithsburg's in-town homes are compact and older, its farms are working fruit operations, and the calls divide cleanly between the two: rooflines and chimneys in town, burrows and buildings out on the mountain roads.

faqs.q: Are rattlesnakes really around Clear Spring?
faqs.a: Timber rattlesnakes occur in the rocky mountain country of western Washington County, and the ridges near Clear Spring are within their Maryland range — sightings are uncommon but real. They are protected, cannot be killed or possessed by an operator, and are handled as a safety matter: keep people and animals away, note the location, and get advice before anyone works that ground. Copperheads are the more likely venomous encounter in the valley's rocky and wooded edges, and those we can capture without harm and release on site or within two miles as Maryland law allows. Most snakes on a Clear Spring farm, though, are black rat snakes — and those are worth keeping.

Clear Spring.wildlife_intro:
Clear Spring is a small town in western Washington County, set in the Conococheague valley farming country between Hagerstown and the Potomac River bends. It is limestone valley Maryland — rich farm soil, spring runs, orchards and pastures — and its wildlife work is the valley-farm set with a mountain accent from the ridges nearby.

Groundhogs lead, burrowing the field edges, orchard rows, and under the barns and sheds of the area's farms, and under the porches of the in-town homes at the field margins. Raccoons den in the older chimneys and commute the creek bottoms; skunks work the lawns and den under outbuildings; bats take the tall farmhouse attics in summer. The rocky ridges west of town hold copperheads, and timber rattlesnakes occur in the mountain ground — protected, and strictly a safety and referral matter. Black rat snakes are the common barn snake, protected and useful. Clear Spring properties are mostly working properties, and the pattern holds: one walked visit, the house sealed, the burrows mapped and trapped, and the outbuildings screened, in a priority order set with the owner on the spot.
